title: Mesut Barış Övün: Günizleri (37)
desc: Gönderen: Enis Batur’u okuyorum, on üç yıl sonra yeniden. Bu kez aradan geçen süreyi net olarak verebiliyorum, çünkü hatırlıyorum: IELTS sınavı için İstanbul’a gitmiştim. Birkaç kitabevi seferi de yap...
content:
Gönderen: Enis Batur’u okuyorum, on üç yıl sonra yeniden. Bu kez aradan geçen süreyi net olarak verebiliyorum, çünkü hatırlıyorum: IELTS sınavı için İstanbul’a gitmiştim. Birkaç kitabevi seferi de yapmıştım tabii, dönüş yolunda yanımdaki kitaplar arasındaydı Gönderen, oradan biliyorum (aldığım kitapların ilk sayfasına tarih yazma alışkanlığını hâlâ edinebilmiş değilim.) Hemen otobüste başlamıştım kitaba, biraz şaşkınlık ve merakla; muhtemelen böyle tematik bir deneme kitabı daha önce okumamıştım. Enis Batur, ismini çok duyduğum ama birkaç dergi yazısı dışında yapıtına yabancı olduğum bir yazardı. Gönderen’i çok sevdim, hakkında blogumda bir yazı da yayımladım. Sonra diğer kitapları geldi: Bu Kalem Bukalemun, Bu Kalem Melun, Merak Cemiyeti Tutanakları, Rakım Sıfır, Ada Günlükleri, Kitap Evi ve daha nicesi. Sanırım zamanla ben de sokulgan bir okur oldum. Şu an kitaplığımda en çok kitabı bulunan yazar odur.

Çok sevdiğiniz ama kimseye tavsiye etmediğiniz, edemediğiniz yazarlar olur. Enis Batur benim için böyledir. Aslen herhâlde şair olduğunu söylemek gerekir. Ama o, “yazı beyi” der kendine. Doğrusu, şiire çok emek vermiştir, yazarak ve hakkında yazarak bu türde derin ve kapsamlı bir külliyat oluşturmuştur. Ben şiirine o kadar yakın değilim ama düzyazılarına bayılırım. Onu benim için özel kılan şey pek kimselere benzemeyen üslubudur. Bu yazılar deneme, günlük, anı, düzyazı şiir, öykü ve minimal öykü türleri arasında salınır durur; tekniklerin iç içe geçtiği parlak ve cesur metinlerdir. Bir arkadaşıma Acı Bilgi’den bahsederken (kitabı önerirken değil) “üstünde roman yazıyor, aldanma!” demişimdir. Enis Batur yazılarında bu konuyu da işlemeyi sever, klasik tür tanımlarına meydan okurcasına yazar ve bu tip metinlerini TYN diye isimlendirir: Tanımlanamayan Yazınsal Nesne.

Birkaç dergi yazısı dedim, biri Aktüel’deydi ve aslında o da bir mektuptu. Enis Bey, Francesco Petrarca’ya, yaklaşık yedi yüz yıl önce yaşamış bu İtalyan ozana sesleniyordu. Küçük bir şok yaşamıştım; demek edebiyatta böyle şeyler yapılabiliyordu! Ve doğrusu şahane bir mektuptu o gönderilen.

Ben mektup fikrini de bu sözcüğün kendisini de çok severim. Yazarım da. Günizleri arşivi editörlere, arkadaşlarıma ya da anonim okurlara yazılmış mektuplarla doludur. Bugün mail formatında olsalar, öyle gönderilseler de onlar da birer mektuptur şüphesiz. Bir mektubu yazarken özenir, bir öyküye çalışır gibi üstüne çalışırım. O yüzden taslaklarda haftalarca bekleyen mektuplarım olur. Bundan başka, yıllar önce Öykülem’de çıkan ilk hikâyem Mektuplar Kalsaymış, ikinci öykü dosyamın da adıdır şu an.

Bu konuda son bir not: Gönderen: Enis Batur’u ele aldığım blog yazımda kitabı övmüş ve yazınsal bir tür olarak mektuptan da sevgiyle bahsetmiştim. O yazı “E, Elmanın İçi de henüz okuma yazma bilmeyen bir çocuğa yazılmış bir mektup değil mi, şunun şurasında?” diye biter.

***

Sait Faik Hikâye Armağanı’nı alamam ama belki kısa listeye kalabilirim (umut yazarın ekmeğidir). Peki, ne olur bunun sonucunda, böyle bir “derece” acaba yazan kişiye ne getirir? Kısa listeye kalmak şüphesiz bir öne çıkmadır bu yolculukta, yeni bir adımdır; artık ileriye mi yukarıya mı, bunu zaman gösterecektir. Benim asıl takıldığım nokta şu: Böyle bir durum yazı masasını nasıl etkiler? Yani elimdeki dosyalar, gönderdiklerim, bitirdiğim ve bekleyen metinlerimin seyri hızlanır da işler bir nebze olsun kolaylaşır mı acaba benim için?

Bilemiyorum. Geçmişte aksi yönde pek çok örnek olduğu için kesin bir şey söylemek zor. Yani bırakın kısa listeyi, zamanında ödül ya da ödüller alan tanınmış yazarların bile yeni kitapları için yayıncı bulmakta sorun yaşadıkları olmuş. Demek ödüller ya da listeler işleri her zaman hızlandırmıyor. Böyle bir garanti yok. Ama karamsar olmak da benim yapımda yok. Her zaman bir “neyse ki” hali içindeyim. Ben elimdeki dosyaların, bekleyen yazılarımın bu vesileyle önünün açılabileceğini düşünmek istiyorum.

Ama tabii hiçbir şey olmasa da bir şey olabilir: Kitabın editörü kitabı ciddiye almaya başlayabilir!

***

Disney Plus’ta Bruce Springsteen’in bir dönemini anlatan Deliver Me From Nowhere’i izledim. Film, bütün bir kariyer yerine sanatçının üne yeni yeni kavuştuğu ve bazı psikolojik sorunlar yaşadığı kısa bir zaman dilimine odaklanarak farklı bir şey yapıyor. Bruce’un menajeri Jon Landau ile olan arkadaşlığı ve aralarındaki güven duygusu iyi verilmiş. Hikâyede bir şey özellikle dikkatimi çekiyor. Bruce Springsteen, 1982 yılında çıkan albümü Nebraska öncesinde yapımcısına bir şart koşuyor: “Radyo yok, tur yok, basın yok! Bu albüm kendi başına nefes almalı!”

Bu bakımdan, Springsteen’in “Bu albüm kendi başına nefes almalı” demesi beni gülümsetti.

***

Doğrusu Yann Martel tanıdığım bir yazar değil. Pi’nin Yaşamı’nı okumadığım gibi bir dönem ses getiren ünlü filmi de izlemedim. Ama Martel’in kurallar ya da yazmayı öğrenme konusunda söylediklerini benimsedim.

Pera Palas’taki kokteylde Selçuk Altun’un yanına gittim: Birlikte bir fotoğraf çektirebilir miyiz? Biraz muzip ve babacan bir tavırla sordu: Neden? Çünkü dedim, ben sizin okurunuzum. Öyle mi? Tabii tabii, Kitap İçin’lerin hepsini okudum. Selçuk Bey bunun üzerine biraz yaklaşıp, peki söyle bakalım, dedi, yayımlanan son romanımın adı ne? O an, ders sırasında aniden soru yönelttiğim öğrencilerimin yaşadığı tedirginliği daha iyi anladım! İsmini bilmeme ve hatta hakkında birkaç inceleme yazısı da okumuş olmama rağmen bu son kitabın adını hatırlayamadım. Bir an bir sessizlik oldu, ben de tamamen boş olmadığımı göstermek için, genelde bir dize seçiyorsunuz kitap adı olarak, dedim. Selçuk Bey beni fazla mahcup hissettirmek istemediği için olacak, romanın adını kendi söyledi: Öpsem Öldürürler Öpmesem Öldüm. Aa, evet ya, dedim ve bu ismin de Karacaoğlan’ın bir şiirinden mülhem olduğunu ekledim. Sanırım bu bilgi sayesinde biraz kanaat notu kazandım. O da az ötede elinde telefonuyla bekleyen ve bu garip diyalogu anlamaya çalışan Nilay’a dönerek, hadi çekelim bakalım, dedi. Birlikte gülümseyerek poz verdik. Benim için hoş ve komik bir anı oldu. Az sonra fotoğrafı gönderdiğim bir arkadaşım saadetimin gözlerimden okunduğunu yazdı bana.

Mesut Barış Övün

title: James Joyce'un Bebek İzlenimleri ve Edebi Biyografinin Diğer “Garip Zevkleri”
desc:
In the Lake District, 1994.
Each week, The Paris Review unlocks stories, poems, and interviews for our readers from our archive. This week, we’ve unlocked our interview with Hermione Lee, selected fro...
content:
In the Lake District, 1994.

Each week, The Paris Review unlocks stories, poems, and interviews for our readers from our archive. This week, we’ve unlocked our interview with Hermione Lee, selected from the archive by Daisy Hildyard, whose story “Two Lives” appears in our recent Summer issue. Sign up for the Redux newsletter to receive these pieces to your inbox every Sunday morning.

Everybody dabbles in biography. If you have ever spoken at a funeral, rewritten your CV, or gossiped, you’ve had to deal with some of the questions that Hermione Lee discusses with Louisa Thomas in her Art of Biography interview. What is the shape of a life? What are the ingredients of an achievement? What specific person and what particular circumstances produced it? When something fails, do we have to find somebody to blame? Lee addresses these questions as matters of technique: the work of finding, or inventing, “a structure that is sympathetic to the subject.”

There is a kind of mise en abyme at play in her work, and in this interview about the life of somebody who writes the lives of those who captured something of life in their writing. Literary biography is an awkward pleasure. I like its strange textures and surprises. You catch James Joyce doing his impressions of a baby, or spend the summer with Tolstoy when he is on one of his horse yogurt diets. I believed I had a fair understanding of W. G. Sebald until I read his biography and saw the black-and-white snapshot of him as a young man standing thigh-deep in a river, topless in wet jeans with a deep tan, defined muscles, and a dagger in his hand. I also enjoy the genre for its practical insights. It’s useful to know how other writers chased their invoices, or when their children napped.

Lee’s biographies are exceptional for their integration of original research with illuminating interpretations of the authors’ works, and they last. I’ve read and reread her Penelope Fitzgerald and Virginia Woolf; I’ve used the footnotes and followed her sources. I still have my mother’s twenty-nine-year-old Virago Press paperback Willa Cather. I can’t think of another writer, biographer or otherwise, who reads as closely as Lee, or with the same balance and imagination.

In their searching conversation, I was particularly interested in what Lee and Thomas have to say about the undisclosed elements of a life, including Lee’s own (she is reticent). They discuss lies and secrets. They also discuss inventiveness and hard work. The interview leaves me with a sense of how much it takes to make a sincere attempt to understand another person’s life.

 

The Art of Biography No. 4
Hermione Lee, interviewed by Louisa Thomas

INTERVIEWER

Do you find that you read biographies and think, This person is falling in love with his or her subject?

LEE

There are some figures, aren’t there, who seem to attract a certain kind of emotive treatment. Woolf is certainly one of them, Plath is another, Lawrence is another. Or, biography can be a form of rescue operation, special pleading. Painted Shadow: A Life of Vivienne Eliot, by Carole Seymour-Jones, is a good example of that. It has to demonize T. S. Eliot in order to do its job of rescuing his first wife. Biography has so much to do with blame. It is not a neutral zone. So you will get biographies of Woolf where Leonard is blamed, or where her half brothers, George and Gerald Duckworth, are blamed, or where her father, Leslie Stephen, is blamed. It’s as if you can’t tell a life story without someone having to be blamed. Named and shamed and blamed.

From issue no. 205 (Summer 2013)

Elli kuruş ve on saat, dedi.
Öteki işçiler de aynı fikirdeydiler.
Derin, felsefi bir fikir değil elbet.
Fakat tehlikeli bir fikir.

Memleketimden İnsan Manzaları’nı okuyorum. Adını bundan fazla hak eden bir kitap var mıdır acaba? Ne ararsanız var: İşçiler, mahkûmlar, jandarmalar, köylüler, sinsi politikacılar, avantacılar, asker kaçakları, vurguncular, Kartallı Kâzım, canım ciğerim işçi Kerim, Basri Şener, Burhan Özedar, Kambur Kerim, Şevki Bey (Orhan Kemal’in babasına çok benzer), karaborsacılar… Daha neler neler: II. Meşrutiyet ve Abdülhamid, Hitler, Adana İğtişaşı, 31 Mart, mahpushaneler, tren garları ve istasyonlar, Garson Mustafa ve Aşçıbaşı Mahmut Aşer…

Fakat bir tanesi var ki bilhassa kayda değer. Kötülüğün vücut bulmuş hali: Şahende Hanım.

Haydarpaşa’dan 15.45’te kalkan katarın 510 numaralı üçüncü mevki vagonunun kadınlar bölmesi. En ihtiyarları pencerenin solunda oturuyor: rahmetli Şerif ağanın karısı Şahende Hanım. Ölen oğluna acımamış olan, ömründe zaten hiçbir şeye acımamış olan ve bu dünyada hiç kimseyi sevmemiş olan Şahende Hanım.

Vagondaki gebe kadın tatsın diye, bir sepet dolusu kirazından isterler Şahende Hanım’dan. Birkaç kere seslenirler, sağır mıdır acaba teyze? Yoo, değildir.

Şahende Hanım
kalın kemikleriyle yeldirmesinin içinden sıyrılır gibi
ağır ağır kalktı yerinden,
indirdi sepeti kınalı elleriyle rafın üzerinden
ve açık pencereden dışarı
döktü kirazları.
Sonra boş sepeti eski yerine yerleştirip
ve tekrar kalın kemikleriyle siyah yeldirmesinin içine girip oturdu.
Eski şapkası sarsılarak ağlıyordu gebe kadın.

5 Mayıs 2026

Yedinci’ye

Sabah çok erken kalktık, yola koyulduk. Güneş daha yüzünü göstermemişti ama kızıllığı vuruyordu ovaya. Evet, önümüzde uzun ve sıska bir ova vardı. Sarıdan bıktıracak denli yoğun bir bozkır sarısı kaplamıştı yeri göğü. Dünya her günkü doğumunu yeniden, sanki ilk defaymışçasına yaşıyordu. Güneşin doğuşu değildi sadece doğum. Doğanın, yani hayvanların ağaçların otların ve suların yeniden uyanmasıydı.

Ovayı üç günde geçtik. Gündüzleri yol alıyor, güneş gidince duruyorduk. Kalabalık bir grup değildik aslında ama kendimizi kalabalık sayıyorduk. Güçsüz, yalnız hissetseydik çoktan ölmüştük.

Ovadan sonra orman başladı. Gümbür gümbür bir orman. İçinde binbir çeşit canlı. Görünen ve görünmeyen bedenler, konuşan rüzgâr ve ıslık çalan dallar. Çok dikkatli olmak zorundaydık, olduk da.

Ormandaki ikinci günümüzdü galiba, karşımıza dev cüceler çıktı. Bunlar ilk bakışta zararsız gibi görünüyorlardı. Dev gibi olduklarından habersizdiler. Belki onların lugatında devlik-cücelik yoktu. Bunu hiç soramadık onlara. Çünkü görüp görebileceğimiz en ukala, kendini beğenmiş varlıklardı bu dev cüceler. Bir hikmet yumurtluyormuş gibi büyük büyük laflar ediyorlardı habire. Araya girip günlük işlerden bahsedemiyorduk. Basit şeylere, basit, güzel ama gerçek şeylere sıra gelmiyordu bir türlü. Hikmet gibi görünen sözlerinin ne kadar boş olduğunu anlamamız çok uzun sürmedi. Ama yapacak bir şey yoktu, dinledik. Sanattan, edebiyattan, zamandan ve ölümden konuşup durdular. Sözleri boştu, çünkü anlamları yoktu. Ahkâm kesmek bir spor olsaydı bu adamların hepsinin altın madalyaları olurdu. Kırk gün kırk gece süren bu boş sohbetten sonra yola koyulduk yeniden. Artık biraz daha büyümüştük, sabır kaslarımız epey gelişmişti.

Kasabalardan da geçtik. Bazısında aylarca kaldığımız oluyordu. Bazen bir çay içip kalkıyorduk.

Yapıyorduk, ediyorduk, falan filan. Peki, “biz” kimdik? Biz okula gitmemiş, öğrendiğimiz her şeyi işte böyle gezip dolanarak öğrenmiş olan tuhaf bir gruptuk. Altı erkek, bir kadındık. Yıllardır yürüyorduk. Okula gitmemiştik, çalışmıyorduk, çoluk çocuğumuz yoktu (ve olmayacaktı). Herhangi bir sınır, bayrak ve din aidiyetimiz de yoktu. Fakat gelmiş geçmiş tüm peygamberlerin hayatını merak eder, onların davranışlarından kendimize dersler çıkarırdık. Bununla birlikte kilise, havra, cami, cemevi ya da başka herhangi bir tapınağa ancak turistik nedenlerle girerdik. İbadet için değil.

Bazı yerlerde iyi karşılanıyorduk, ama çok başımıza gelen bir şey değildi bu.

İnsanın iyi olduğuna inanmak istiyorduk. Her şey aksini işaret etse de.

Günün birinde, istenmeyen ama beklenen şey oldu. Ayrıldık. Herkes dört bir yana dağıldı.

Ben işte burada, dağ başındaki bu kulübedeyim. Artık pek okumuyorum, yazmıyorum da. Ama size bu mektubu göndermek istedim canım efendim.

Anlattığım her şeyi siz zaten biliyorsunuz. Olsun, hatırlatmak istedim.

Gözlerinizden, ellerinizden öperim.

7 Mayıs 2026

Arz-talep

Ben ekonomist değilim, hiç anlamam para pul işlerinden, istatistiklerden, arzdan talepten. Fakat iş anlaşılmayacak gibi değil.

Evvelsi yıl yaptığımız Parşömen yılsonu soruşturmasında (Parşömen 2024 Edebiyat Soruşturması) 7 yıldır devam eden soruşturmalarda ilk ve son kez farklı bir soru yer alıyordu: “Düzenli olarak takip ettiğiniz bir edebiyat dergisi var mı?”

O yıl 104 kişi yanıtlamıştı soruşturmayı. Ve yanıtlayanların ezici çoğunluğunun düzenli olarak edebiyat dergisi takip etmediği, okumadığı bir anlamda kayda geçmişti. Basılı dergi çıkaran arkadaşlarda durum nasıl bilmiyorum ama erişimi ücretsiz ve çok kolay olmasına rağmen Parşömen de artık çok az okunuyor. Öyle ki Parşömen’de yazısı yayımlanan biri bana yazısının kaç kez okunduğunu (tıklandığını) sorduğunda ben mahcup oluyorum o rakamı söylemeye. Parşömen 20. yılında. Hiç bu kadar az ilgi görmemişti, hiç bu kadar az okunmamıştı yayımlanan metinler.

Bunda belki Parşömen’in yayın politikasının etkisi vardır. Öykü ve şiir yayımlamıyor oluşumuzun da etkisi çok tabii. Nedenini tam olarak bilmiyorum ama sonuç olarak, talep olmayan yerde arza devam etmek anlamlı mı? Ciddi ciddi düşünmek lazım.

Bir süredir ciddi ciddi düşünüyorum ben de. O nedenle bir önceki Dünlük’te (Dünlük 249, 11 Mart 2026), biraz da ümitsizce ve belki de kendime fazla vurarak şöyle yazmıştım: “Peki, yükten ve angaryadan başka bir şeye benzemeyen bir dergiye (bir tek sen dergi diyorsun ona, bildiğin site işte, web-sitesi) insan neden bu kadar uzun süre emek verir? Kendine eziyet etmeyi hobi mi bellemiştir?”

Bana kalırsa bir edebiyat dergisinin asli görevi yeni yazarlara yer vermektir. Geçen 19 yıl boyunca bunu “azıcık” da olsa başardı sanıyorum Parşömen. Bu iyi, ama okunmamak kötü. Az okunmak iyi değil. (Yanlış anlama olmasın, tıklanma ya da okunma sayısının bana maddi bir getirisi yok. Parşömen’in hiçbir anlamda bana para getirisi yok zaten.)

Benim yukarıdaki sorularım Hasan Orhan’ı uzun uzun düşündürmüş, Libre Kültür’de yayımlanan yazısını yazmasına neden olmuş. Bu güzel yazıyı şöyle bitirmiş Hasan Orhan:

Aslında olan biten, yazarından okuruna herkesin kendine bir yer açma çabasıdır. Onur Çalı’nın sorduğu o “yük ve angarya” dergiciliğin ta kendisidir. Eğer dergi, okurunu bir yazarın zihnine ya da bir dosyanın ortasına yerleştirebiliyorsa, yazanın öngörülemezliğinden bir “yazar” kimliği damıtabiliyorsa; en geniş ifadeyle kamusal vazifesini “azıcık” da olsa göğüsleyebiliyorsa, o angarya editörün kadri bilinmediği durumlarda dahi en kıymetli mesaisine dönüşür. Editörlerin sitemi, yazar ve okurların sessizliği ya da öfkesi… Öyle yahut böyle, hepsi de mutfağın kokusudur. Başkalarını bilemem, ben o mutfaktan yayılan kokunun peşinde, bir yazanı keşfetmenin heyecanı ve rastlantıların tekinsiz ama cazibeli sularında, sefalet içinde sürünse de günceli yoklamak için, bu angarya işlerle ilgilenmeye devam edeceğim.

Birileri muhakkak devam edecek tabii.

Ama miadı dolanların da sahneyi terk etmeyi bilmesi gerekir.

10 Mayıs 2026

“Günlerimiz kime ait?”

Paolo Sorrentino’nun yeni filmi La Grazia’nın kahramanı Mariano De Santis şöyle diyor filmin sonlarına doğru:

Kızım Dorotea, bir gün şu soruyu sordu bana: “Günlerimiz kime ait?” Cevap çok bariz. Bize ait. Ama çelişki bu ya, (bunu) anlamaya ömrümüz yetmiyor.

Enfes bir film La Grazia. Yaşlılık, yalnızlık, pişmanlık, ihanet, bağışlama, dostluk, ebeveynlik, yaşam, ölüm üzerine zarif bir görsel şiir.

Onur Çalı

Dünlük 250: “Günlerimiz kime ait?” yazısı ilk önce Parşömen üzerinde ortaya çıktı.

title: Helen Mirren, Patricia Highsmith'i mi oynuyor?! A Talent for Murder fragmanını izleyin.
desc:

The film stars Alde...
content:
This morning, fans of both Patricia Highsmith and Dame Helen Mirren have cause to rejoice. The trailer for Anton Corbijn’s new Ripley-adjacent film, A Taste for Murder, is out now.

The film stars Alden Ehrenreich, Olivia Cooke, and an almost unrecognizable Helen Mirren. It follows a thirsty agent (Ehrenreich) who heads to the Swiss hinterlands to convince Highsmith (Mirren!) to write one last installment of her famous Ripley series. But things—as they tend to, in the Highsmith universe—take a dark turn.

Here’s the trailer.

 

A Talent for Murder is itself an adaptation, of the 2014 play Switzerland by Joanna Murray-Smith. Switzerland imagines Highsmith as a recluse in the Alps, closely guarding a cache of weapons and secrets after a lifetime spent writing mysteries.

The play enjoyed runs in Bristol, Sydney, and Los Angeles. Murray-Smith is adapting her own script for the screen version.

This project joins a long line of Ripley adaptations. A bevy of international auteurs—including René Clément, Wim Wenders, and Anthony Minghella—have taken a pass at old Tom and his creator. The dark-hearted con man last received the screen treatment in a Netflix adaptation starring Andrew Scott. But we’re originalists, over here.

One thing’s certain. It will be exciting to see how a focus on Highsmith can draw some fresh blood from this story, which historically hinges on the magnetic cipher at its center. And obviously, we’ve gotta see what Dame Helen’s up to.

Look for the film in theaters on October 23.

title: Tim Curry'nin Pennywise'ının neşeli dehşetine bir övgü
desc: Tim Curry, who died this week at 80, will probably always be best known for his performance as Dr. Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, and not unreasonably. With his snug corset and unsub...
content:
Tim Curry, who died this week at 80, will probably always be best known for his performance as Dr. Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, and not unreasonably. With his snug corset and unsubtle make-up and minuscule shorts to which are fastened fishnet stockings, Curry’s kooky scientist with a penchant for  brewing male lovers in his lab is one of pop-culture’s unlikely icons. Frank-N-Furter exists in the gap between the counter culture and punk, the child of classic musicals and 1930s B-movies. The performance is daringly weird, perverse and outlandish, seductively charming, and, for all the flamboyance, Curry never veers out of control, never takes it too far. With his gender-defying garb and the way he gleefully flaunts his sexuality, Frank-N-Furter is an inimitable figure, unburdened by shame. And this strange, beseeching man who proudly eschews the mainstream’s prissy morals isn’t an outcast: he rules over a large, diverse assembly of hired help and acolytes who seem, largely, to like him. In any case, they’re content enough spontaneously break into carefully choreographed musical numbers. He’s a mad scientist, but Curry plays him as something more interesting, something weirder, than a villain.

Curry’s genius is that he shows us how fun and liberating embracing the weird can be. He admires how the Transylvanian just acts like himself. But my favorite Tim Curry performance will always be Pennywise, the clown in Tommy Lee Wallace’s 1990 miniseries adaptation of Stephen King’s It, which, compared to Andy Muschietti’s mega popular pair of films, is modest, even a little lame. The miniseries is only three hours long, so Wallace had to heavily truncate King’s gargantuan tome, curtailing and expunging scenes and entire characters, as well as toning things down to fit broadcast rules.

But Wallace uses this hindrance as inspiration for creative ways of translating King’s writing to the small screen. You can see it from the very beginning. The first chapter of the novel is one of the scariest things King has ever written. It’s smartly structured, the details with which he describes the scene are astute and intense, the prose is lovely and melancholy and mostly free of the sloppy redundancies and annoying colloquial tics that King loves a little too much, the two young brothers are efficiently and empathetically fleshed out so we are quickly invested in them, and when the horror, which he portends, does arrive, it’s not just shocking, but tragic. The miniseries is basically the same.

It’s a rainy day, and a young boy wearing a yellow raincoat chases a boat made of newspaper floating down a gutter alive with flowing rain. The boat falls into a sewer, and, as the boy goes to retrieve it, a face appears out of darkness—a clown, with spotless, uncanny white skin, a bulbous red nose, and untamed red hair. In his Bronx accent, he talks affably to the boy, magnanimously returning his boat and asking him to play. Soon enough, he tears the boy’s arm off and leaves him to die in the gutter. In the miniseries, this is implied, following the decree of network TV standards circa 1990, but it’s still scary because Curry almost convinces us that he is a nice clown, a friend, even though he is lurking in a sewer. When his insidious nature is revealed, the change in tone and his face gone malformed, the scene feels dynamic in a way that doesn’t require gore or intricate special effects. Here and throughout the film, we see how he has fun betraying a child’s trust and ruining his innocence, which is maybe an even more profound violence than dismemberment. The shape-shifting eldritch entity of mysterious origins relishes torturing children. He takes many forms, but likes being a clown the best. It’s a nasty irony. As King writes, “The fears of children could often be summoned up in a single face… and if bait were needed, why, what child did not love a clown?”

“The clown may be the source of mirth, but—who shall make the clown laugh?” Angela Carter wrote in Nights at the Circus. Pennywise, naturally, makes himself laugh.

While Muschietti’s films are far more faithful translations of King’s opus narratively, having the freedom of an R rating, a big budget, and twice as much time as the miniseries to tell the story, they rely on generic creepy imagery and ostentatious scare tactics, expensive banality. Bill Skarsgård plays Pennywise with relentless menace. There is little nuance and few surprises. Compare Curry’s Pennywise to Bill Skarsgård’s: Skarsgård looks and sounds unequivocally evil from the beginning, whereas Curry actually has the mannerisms of a clown you might find at a kid’s backyard birthday party. That juxtaposition makes him scary and exciting. Curry knew that in order to scare kids, he first has to appeal to them, inveigle them with his deceitful promise of friendship, earn their trust with kindness, all smiles, and speak to them in playful words—speak their own language. As Lovecraft says in “The Outsider,” “Unhappy is he to whom the memories of childhood bring only fear and sadness.” This may be why as adults, the Losers Club forget their childhood horrors: so they can save their own lives. If you can’t get your innocence back, maybe you can at least rid yourself of the memory of what took it from you.

And, unlike Bill Skarsgård’s, Curry’s Pennywise is having fun. His taunts and emotional torture are unsettling yet also profane fun because he delivers them in the tone of a friend busting your chops. When he appears in the library, invisible to all but our lead character, he has a hoot practicing his standup. “The clown may be the source of mirth, but—who shall make the clown laugh?” Angela Carter wrote in Nights at the Circus. Pennywise, naturally, makes himself laugh.

The image of him, his attire a blasphemous betrayal of the wholesome fun a clown costume promises, and with vibrant, colorful balloons in his hand, lingers in our minds for a long time. He appears on screen for less than 20 minutes, yet it feels like he is always there. In his absence, we still sense his danger. He is all the characters think about.

We can contrast Curry’s clown to another supernatural villain he played, Darkness in Legend, mythic under the prosthetics, delivering in his deep demonic voice cryptic proclamations. And yet, Darkness has a romantic side, too: he is attracted to the innocence of a beautiful young woman, and wants to marry her. (Though he uses dark magic to woo her, which to him is an acceptable declaration of love.) When he is vanquished at the end, he reminds Tom Cruise’s hero that evil lurks in all living things, so while his corporeal presence may die, his essence lives on.

Pennywise—or rather, It—has terrorized the small simple town of Derry, Maine for who knows how long, generation after generation born and dead as he remains lurking in nightmares, manipulating his victims, making real their deepest fears because he knows them so well. King’s best writing has an earnest intimacy. What makes him one of the great writers of adolescents is the respect with which he portrays the kids’ vulnerable moments, their hopes, their shame, their fears.

Too often, horror has gradually come to think that if a film wants to be taken seriously, its bad guys, however wicked, however sadistic, man or monster, whatever their motivation (if they even have one), should be austere. Humor is unbecoming. Tim Curry had no such delusions; he understood that scary can be fun, and fun can provoke fear. When Pennywise cracks a joke, the contrast of his antics with the scary stuff can be more impactful, have more personality, than just scare after scare. It’s a skill to control tone and tempo and cadence. And when Pennywise enjoys the horror he evokes, his laugh can perturb more deeply and last more clearly in your memory than a simple jumpscare or spilled blood. You don’t forget Pennywise telling a kid, “Kiss me, fat boy!” and neither does the kid, who is embarrassed by his weight, gets teased about it; years later, as a slender, successful adult, when the long-buried memories of Derry come back, it’s that quip and the clown’s guffaw he remembers.

title: Terk Edilemeyen Duvarlardan Kötü İnanç ve Büyük Ötekine: “Bir Şair” Filmi Üzerine
desc:
Aslınur Arısoy
Simón Mesa Soto’nun 2025 yapımı Un Poete (“Bir Şair”) filmi, bir sanatçının yaratamama sancısının yanı sıra narsisistik olarak hırpalanmış egosunu da ekrana yansıtır. Başrol oyuncusunun...
content:
Aslınur Arısoy

Simón Mesa Soto’nun 2025 yapımı Un Poete (“Bir Şair”) filmi, bir sanatçının yaratamama sancısının yanı sıra narsisistik olarak hırpalanmış egosunu da ekrana yansıtır. Başrol oyuncusunun (Ubeimar Rios) beden postüründen ağır ifadelerine, sahnelerin çerçevelenişinden karakterin ilerlemekte zorlandığı ve yer yer donakaldığı sekanstaki tercihlere baktığımızda; filmin genel anlatı dili, varoluşsal ketlenmenin trajikomik debelenişi duygusunu izleyiciye estetik biçimde iletmektedir. Oscar karakterinin dinamiğine odaklanan bu yazı, yaratıcılık krizini Sartre’ın “Kötü İnanç”ı ve Lacan’ın “Büyük Öteki”si ekseninde ele almayı denemektedir.

İçinden Çıkılamayan Anne Evleri: Çözülemeyen Ödipal Bağlar

Oscar boşanmış bir baba olarak anne evine geri dönmüştür. Film boyunca da, ne zaman eyleme geçmeye, evden çıkmaya yeltense “başarısız” olmakta ve yeniden anne evine sığınmaktadır. O ev onu kapsayan ve belki de bütünlük yanılsaması veren yegâne yerdir. Eve dönmediği zamanlarda, bir kaldırımın kenarında sızan atıl bir nesne görünümünde, bedensel öznelliğini neredeyse kaybetmektedir. Onun evden her ayrılışı benzer bir döngüyü izlemektedir, evlenip boşanmak ya da 24 gibi genç bir yaşta ödül alıp sonrasında üretemez olmak hali de benzer bir örüntüyü düşündürmektedir.

Evin içerisinde Oscar’ın yetişkin olmasını ve sorumluluk almasını talep eden kişi ablasıdır. Anne karakteri, ablasının yasa koyuculuğuna karşın, “Sıcak çikolata ister misin?” sorusu ile daha da emin olduğumuz, Oscar’a dışarıyı işaret etmekten ziyade, onu içeride tutmaya meyleden kişidir. Annesi psikolojik anlamda, farkında olarak ya da olmayarak, Oscar’ın sütten kesilmesine de pek müsaade etmemektedir. Annenin bu boğucu kapsayıcılığı Oscar’ı eksiksiz ama aynı zamanda eylemsiz bir “özne-nesne” olarak içeride tutmaktadır. Oscar bu evde konforlu bir acı içerisinde yıkıcı bir jouissance üretmektedir.

José Asunción Silva, lanetli şair, Oscar için Latin Amerika’nın en büyük şairidir. Odasının duvarına asılan portrenin Silva’ya ait olması tabii rastgele değildir. Oscar kendisini onun “ölümsüzleşmeyi başarmış” bakışlarına maruz bırakır. Silva’nın duvara çakılı bakışı, Oscar için ilham verici gibi gözükse de ziyadesiyle kastratiftir. Oscar yazamama halini kendi sorumluluğu olarak görmektense trajik ve dışsal bir kader olarak romantize eder. Bu ise tam anlamıyla Sartre’ın “kötü inanç” (Mauvaise Foi) kavramına işaret etmektedir. Bu inanca kapılıp kendisini nesneleştirmeyi seçmesi ile sorumluluğundan kaçmakta, bedelini özgürlüğü ile ödemektedir. Nihayetinde onun yaratıcılığını yutan şeyler çevresel olduğu kadar varoluşsal felci ve alkolizmidir. Silva, doktoruna kalbinin yerini çizdirir ve ertesi gün o noktadan kendini vurarak yaşamına son verir. Oscar’ı da bir sahnede onu taklit ederken görürüz, “büyüyünce ben de tıpkı babam gibi olacağım” diyen bir çocuğu anımsatan Oscar, göğsüne bir kalp çizer, fakat sembolik biçimde kendi canlılığını ısrarlı bir şekilde sekteye uğratsa da devamı gelmeyecektir. Yazamadıkça, bedeniyle sızar ve bedenine çizer…

Oscar yastan ziyade derin bir melankolinin içerisindedir. Kendi yasını tanımlayamaz ve kaybettiğinin ne olduğunu bilemeden, kendiliğinin bir parçası olarak deneyimleyerek acı çeker. Freud “Yas ve Melankoli” makalesinde: “Yasta dünya yoksullaşır ve boşalır; melankolide ise boşalan ve yoksullaşan bizzat kendiliktir” der. Oscar’ın durumunda kayıp, bir kendilik kaybına dönüşmüştür ve Oscar’ın öfkesini kendi egosuna yöneltmiştir. Biraz da bu sebeple alkolizm ve pasif-agresif yıkıcılığı karşısında izleyicinin Oscar’a öfke yönlendirmesi zorlaşmaktadır ve bu duygu yer yer acımayla maskelenmeye de müsaittir.

Kavuşamayan İki Yaka

Oscar’ın zihninde birbirine kavuşamayan iki kendilik imajı bulunmaktadır. Bunlardan biri “bir şair olmak” temsilinin hakkını veren bir şair olmakken; diğeri ise 40 yaşında olmasına rağmen kızından borç alan, edebiyat camiası tarafından sıradan görülen “başaramamış kişi”dir. Bu ayrık iki imajı bir arada tutmayı denerken düşündüğüm soru şu oluyor: O gerçekten şiir mi yazmak istemektedir yoksa insanların onu bir şair olarak adlandırmasını mı arzulamaktadır? Bu soru da bizleri Lacan’ın “İnsanın arzusu ötekinin arzusudur” fikrine götürmektedir.

Lanetli Şair, Uyumsuz Sanatçılar

Uyumsuz sanatçı anlayışı estetik bir mit gibi dursa da yapısal olarak kaçınılmazdır. Oscar da kendisini konumlandırdığı bu yerde, toplumsal-simgesel düzeni, ekonomik kaygıları olan edebiyat camiasını sözde reddetmektedir. “Büyük Öteki”nin vadettiği sahte bütünlüğü ve yanılsamaları sezmekte, ancak ne bu camiaya yerleşebilmekte ne de tamamen dışarıda var olabilmektedir. Oscar, simgesel düzenin eşiğinde, aidiyetsizliğin getirdiği o arafta dolanıp durmaktadır. Yurdaly ile kurduğu ilişkisi de bu camianın yeniden takdirini alarak belki de oraya yeniden yerleşme, yeniden var olma vaadini bulma çabasıdır. Fakat sanatçı, doğası gereği, sahte uzlaşıları reddeden “yerleşik olmayandır”.

İnsan, yaşından bağımsız olarak, ne zaman narsisistik bir yara alsa, ne zaman değersiz ya da parçalanmış hissetse; kendisini bütün, muhteşem ve eksiksiz hissettirecek yeni “aynalar” (mevkiler, partnerler, hayranlık dolu bakışlar) arar ve bu ilkel ayna evresi illüzyonunu yeniden tesis etme çabasına girer. Oscar’ın, bu sarsılmaların akabinde ablasının bulduğu öğretmenlik işini kabul etmesi ve hemen peşi sıra o “çok yetenekli” öğrencisini keşfetmiş olması da keza rastlantısal değildir. Oscar farkında ya da değil Yurdaly ile ilişkisinde rolleri tersine çevirme imkânı yakalar. Bu kez kendisi, dilin yasasını elinde tutabilir, Yurdaly ise onu “bilen özne” konumuna yerleştirebilir. Fakat Yurdaly şiirin o kadar da kendisine uygun olmadığını görecek ve maddiyatın onun için daha bağlayıcı olduğunu doğruca ifade edecek kadar da otantiktir, şiir onun için araçtır. Yurdaly bu yanıyla Oscar’ın arzusunu askıda tutacağı o gizemli küçük a nesnesi olmayı reddedecek, Oscar’ın onun üzerinden kurduğu düşlemsel ayna hızla çatlayacaktır.

Filmde Yurdaly’nin olduğu gibi olma hali, Oscar için kendi sıradanlığı ve çıplak gerçeğiyle yüzleşmesini sağlayabilecek midir? Devamında Oscar’ın seçimlerini bilmemekle birlikte, bazen sadece kendi otantikliğinde yaşayan insanlarla sahici biçimde ilişkilenmek iki yakayı bir araya toplamayı kolaylaştırabilir mi?

Ve son olarak, acaba bizim duvarlarımızda hangi idealler/idoller asılı; en kamburumuzun çıktığı hallerimizle, biz kimin bakışları ile karşı karşıyayız?

title: Kardeşler, İyi günde Kötü günde
desc: There was a proverb I came across once that’s stuck with me: “If brothers were such a good idea, God would have given himself one.” Harsh, but not untrue. At least as far back as Cain and Abel, the re...
content:
There was a proverb I came across once that’s stuck with me: “If brothers were such a good idea, God would have given himself one.” Harsh, but not untrue. At least as far back as Cain and Abel, the relationship between brothers has proved to be a complicated one, full of petty resentments, jealousies, and competition—but also the unique understanding that only brothers can have, like magnets with the same charge: alike, and therefore repulsed by each other.

If brotherhood can be a burden, it’s especially so for the younger brother. He comes into the world already being measured against the yardstick of his older brother’s accomplishments, often destined by birth order to live in the shadow of a favored firstborn. It leaves him with one of two options: to follow in his older brother’s footsteps without hope of living up to expectations, or to rebel, branching out on his own path to the inevitable disappointment of parents who wish he could be more like his brother. 

My novel Men Like Us explores this dynamic through the Kennedy family. Bobby Kennedy occupies the shaky ground of the younger brother, torn between the pressure to live up to his charming older brother Jack while at the same time trying to develop his own identity independent of his sibling. I wanted to explore what it felt like to be caught between two competing impulses, what it was like to be the “spare,” not the heir, and the expectations and challenges that might come with living your life in the wings instead of on center stage.

For all its faults, the bond between brothers, or any siblings, is the true cradle-to-grave relationship—just as important, in my opinion, as any of the more commonly depicted bonds in literature, between romantic partners or parents and children. Equal parts fraught and exhilarating, brotherhood is a relationship like no other, someone you don’t choose but have to travel alongside through life nonetheless. In the seven books below, we see a variety of brothers and permutations of this thorny relationship—some younger brothers who look up to the older, some who want nothing to do with them, all inextricably bonded to a person who understands them (or doesn’t) like no one else in the world.

Young Mungo by Douglas Stuart

Although ostensibly a queer Romeo and Juliet set in a Glasgow government housing scheme, Young Mungo is also a story about brothers. In Mungo’s world, Protestant and Catholic gangs are at war with each other. Though he has no taste for violence himself, Mungo’s older brother Hamish serves as the leader and general of one of the Protestant gangs. The two brothers are opposites: Mungo is sweet, emotionally perceptive, tender. By contrast, Hamish thinks with his fists, embodying the brash, violent masculinity their world demands for survival. Throughout the novel, Hamish tries to coach Mungo into being more like him, pulling Mungo deeper into gang politics even as Mungo is simultaneously falling for a Catholic boy who lives in the same housing scheme. By the end, the question isn’t whether Mungo will ever be able to follow in his brother’s footsteps, but exactly what it will cost him to do so. 

Salvage the Bones by Jesmyn Ward

Salvage the Bones follows siblings Randall, Skeetah, Esch, and Junior as they prepare for Hurricane Katrina in their rural Mississippi town. Although the novel juggles multiple threads, including the coming storm and Esch’s unexpected pregnancy, one of the most compelling arcs for me centers on Skeetah—the second son—and his place within the family. While his older brother Randall is a talented basketball player whose skill offers a possible route out of their town, Skeetah devotes himself to a completely different path with the same intensity: pitbull fighting. With the two, Ward captures the subtle tension that can exist between younger and older brothers—less an outright, declared rivalry than an unspoken attempt by the younger brother to carve out a unique identity for himself. The result is an understated but no less powerful example of how birth order can shape the identities of brothers themselves. 

Intermezzo by Sally Rooney

Following two brothers in the wake of their father’s death, Intermezzo maps the contentious relationship between younger brother Ivan and older brother Peter as they navigate their grief amidst a lifetime of accumulated misunderstandings. While many books explore the relationship between brothers in childhood, what appeals to me most about this novel is that it spotlights how the sibling relationship evolves—sometimes awkwardly—into adulthood, when the hierarchy established in childhood no longer fits. Peter remains convinced he knows what’s best for Ivan and what “normal” adult life should look like; Ivan resents Peter’s interference and judgement of him. Through Ivan, the book captures the growing pains of being the younger brother and the difficulty of trying to establish your own life while still being seen through the eyes of an older brother who’ll always see you as a child.

The Sisters Brothers by Patrick deWitt

This novel is perfect for anyone with a Western itch to scratch. Assassin brothers Eli and Charlie Sisters are sent by their boss to kill a prospector on his gold mining claim. Along the way, Eli (the younger of the two) begins to question his life as a hitman, a concern that his more aggressive, less introspective brother doesn’t share. The novel tracks their journey (and Eli’s growing doubts) through a series of absurd detours that give the story a picaresque, episodic feel from chapter to chapter. As with Intermezzo, the novel explores what happens when two brothers start to diverge—as well as the bonds between them that, try as they might, can never be severed completely. 

We The Animals by Justin Torres

Told through a series of vignettes, We The Animals follows three brothers who form a “pack”—a bond that’s as intense as it is chaotic—as they come of age in upstate New York. The novel’s unnamed narrator is the youngest of the brothers, a position that leaves him both inside and outside the collective identity he shares with them. Written largely in the first-person plural, the book captures what it feels like to belong so completely to a sibling group that individual identity becomes difficult to separate from it. Yet as the narrator grows older, he starts to discover parts of himself that his brothers can’t share or understand, transforming the story into a powerful exploration of a familiar younger brother dilemma: how to remain connected to the people who shaped you while also becoming distinct from them. 

East of Eden by John Steinbeck

7 Novels About Sibling Rivalries

These characters look to their sisters and brothers with envy and uncertainty, seeking clues as to who they should be

Apr 3 – Lisa Lee
Reading Lists

Set in California’s Salinas Valley, East of Eden centers on the intertwined destinies of the Trask and Hamilton families across multiple generations. A reinterpretation of the story of Cain and Abel, the novel features multiple brother pairings: first Adam and Charles Trask, and later Adam’s twin sons, Aron and Cal. The novel repeatedly returns to the tensions that arise between brothers, particularly when one is cast as the favored son and the other is left to live in the shadow of comparison. Here, Steinbeck transforms one of literature’s oldest stories into a meditation on the burden of being the younger brother: inheriting a place in the family narrative you didn’t ask for and trying, against all odds, to write yourself out of it. 

The Bee Sting by Paul Murray

The Bee Sting tells the story of the Barnes family, who are, like most families, a bit of a mess. Set in Ireland and rotating between the perspective of each family member (Dickie, Imelda, Cass, and PJ), the novel follows the Barnes’ as they fall apart both individually and collectively. One of the things I love most about this novel is that it inverts the expected older brother-younger brother dynamic. Dickie, the older brother, spends much of his early life in the shadow of his more charismatic, athletic younger brother, Frank. Even after Frank’s untimely death, his absence continues to define Dickie and the Barnes family at large, showing how deeply the relationship between brothers can shape how we understand ourselves down the length of our lives.

title: Bu Yaz Okuduğumuz ve Sevdiğimiz 15 Kitap
desc: As you might imagine, we read a lot of books here at EL. Followers of our Instagram may be familiar with our long-running What We’re Reading series, where we post every other week about what staff mem...
content:
As you might imagine, we read a lot of books here at EL. Followers of our Instagram may be familiar with our long-running What We’re Reading series, where we post every other week about what staff members have been reading and loving. Recently, we decided it was time to make this tradition a little more special, and asked staff and interns to share a few thoughts on the books that have been lingering on their nightstands. Below are the titles our team read over the summer—old and new—that excited them the most.

One Leg on Earth by ‘Pemi Aguda

I was in New York on a day when wildfire smoke had settled over the city. Breathing the air, they told us, was like smoking a pack of cigarettes. Needing to be transported somewhere far away, I read Aguda’s strange and beautiful novel. It is set in Lagos (far enough!), a city that is rendered in all its contradictions, chaos, and vitality. Instead of offering escape, the novel reminded me that cities, however different, ask the same impossible thing of us: to build lives alongside one another while the ground beneath us is constantly shifting.

  • Evander Reyes, Communications Director

Names Have Been Changed by Yu-Mei Balasingamchow

I had so much fun reading this whip-fast story of a Singaporean criminal on the run, told in podcast form. As someone who loves the idea of podcasts but is a much better reader than listener, this was perfect for me: all the voice and personality a podcast offers, but on the page instead! I was drawn right in by the narrator’s delightfully irreverent voice and couldn’t stop hitting play on the next episode.

  • Katie Henken Robinson, Deputy Editor

I Can Tell You the Version That Will Make You Take My Side by J Brooke

J Brooke’s debut poetry collection is an incredibly candid look at what it means to be queer in so many contexts: what it means to be part of a family, both of origin and chosen. What it means to move actively in a society that often won’t protect you; what it means to parent a queer child; and what it means to be doing all of this right now, in this version of America. This collection is whip-smart, bursting with heart, and generous with its humor. It’s a quick read, but I loved every second of it.

  • Denne Michele Norris, Executive Director and Publisher

Famous Men by Julie Buntin

I’ve always had a complicated relationship with mentorship. What happens if you tether yourself to a mentor who, ultimately, isn’t who you imagined them to be? This question is at the heart of Famous Men, one Buntin’s protagonist, Will, must navigate on her own. The result is an unflinching portrait of power dynamics, ambition, desires of all kinds, and what happens when a mentor’s voice looms large over your writing and your life—even when you want to escape it. Compelling, gorgeously written, and complex in all the best ways.

  • Katie Henken Robinson, Deputy Editor

The Correspondent by Virginia Evans

I adore epistolary stories and many readers loved this one, so I was curious. From the moment Sybil Van Antwerp carries a mug of Irish breakfast tea with milk to her writing desk, I could feel the concrete details of this world coming vividly to life all around me. There is something so compelling about watching Sybil compose her many letters, rendering her own emotional life with precision that still leaves room for tremendous mystery.

  • Preety Sidhu, Associate Editor, Recommended Reading and The Commuter

Girl’s Girl by Sonia Feldman

Feldman captures a hot, sticky, teenage summer in the suburbs with discerning, literary prose and picture-perfect intensity. I was instantly brought back to my own adolescence: falling asleep in the long grass, giggling over The Sims, dressing up to go to the state fair. The friendships at the heart of Girl’s Girl are endlessly complicated and devastatingly romantic—absolutely true to teenage life.

  • Amulya Tadimety, Editorial Intern

It Could Have Been Her by Lisa Jewell

Another unputdownable psychological jewel(l) of a novel! There’s a missing girl and a house where secrets have calcified across decades. Jewell pulls you into a labyrinth where suspicion clings to everyone inside Thornwood’s walls, and nothing (not even love or blood) feels protective. Her prose moves through layers of lies so deftly that clarity becomes its own trap-you think you’ve found the truth, then question whether you’ve found anything at all. It Could Have Been Her is both unsettling and brilliantly layered, exactly the kind of dark, intricate thriller that proves why l’ve trusted Jewell’s gift for deception since None of This Is True.

  • Shandela Contreras, Editorial Intern

Body Double by Hanna Johansson

Literature is my primary interest, sometimes to the exclusion of everything else. This summer, armed with a Criterion Channel subscription, I decided I wanted to cultivate a deeper appreciation for film . . . and ended up reading Johansson’s novel instead. Body Double is about a consuming romance between two women, one of whom seems to exist only inside their uncanny relationship. It describes itself as a “Hitchcockian thriller”—and I’d argue reading it doubles as a cinematic experience. 

  • Wynter K Miller, Director of Operations and Fiction Editor

London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe

Patrick Radden Keefe uses the story of an upper-middle class family’s tragedy to unpack how extreme foreign wealth—especially the money and business dealings of Russian oligarchs—has been transforming the city of London in recent decades. He is a master storyteller, deftly illuminating deep global backstories and showing how they converge to shape the lives and deaths of the contemporary individuals he is writing about. I am devouring this book and picking up every craft tip I can from it. 

  • Preety Sidhu, Associate Editor, Recommended Reading and The Commuter

Dog Days by Emily LaBarge

I’m typically more of an autofiction reader than a memoir reader, but Dog Days is not your typical memoir. While it takes as its subject a defining personal trauma—LaBarge and her family were held hostage while on holiday—the book doesn’t dwell on the event. Instead, LaBarge circles around it, moving between art, literature, film, and theory. She shifts quickly from one reference to the next, each idea opening onto another, complicating what came before. There are no easy truths about trauma here, no revelation that makes her experience cohere. And yet, reading this book changed me.

  • Evander Reyes, Communications Director

In Other Words by Jhumpa Lahiri

I moved to Italy last year with my family and have been studying the language, so In Other Words—Jhumpa Lahiri’s account of learning Italian—has been on my TBR pile for a while. Lahiri somehow won a Pulitzer, mastered Italian as an adult, and then became so fluent she started writing only in Italian. (Yes, she wrote this book in Italian; Ann Goldstein translated it. My friend . . . save some accomplishments for the rest of us.) It’s a thoughtful, obsessive meditation on language, identity, and the strange joy of becoming a beginner again.

  • Kelly Luce, Editor, The Commuter

Transcription by Ben Lerner

I tend to have a hard time with “COVID fiction.” The pandemic had a near-universal impact, so why can references to masks and quarantine feel so artificial when rendered? I wouldn’t call Transcription a pandemic novel, exactly. It’s a novel about parenthood, mentorship, time and memory, and the failures and foundations of technology. But when COVID does come into play, the personal is made startlingly universal. In Transcription, the pandemic functions less as a discrete event and more as a software; like with technology, Lerner captures how our language, routines, and relationships were forced to adapt or risk obsolescence.

  • Lennie Roeber-Tsiongas, Assistant Editor

Fights! by Scott McClanahan

I began reading about a little boy named Scott mailing his poems with stolen stamps one evening, and finished the same night, crying because I’d finally found a book that knew how I felt after my aunt died. It’s magic when stories that have nothing to do with us become our own. Fights! is about Scott writing books, finding and losing his editor, Gian, his wife, Juliet, and growing into himself. It is a hilarious, wrenching, viscerally intimate novel that I’m rereading already, slower this time.

  • Willem Marx, Associate Editor

Every Time We Say Goodbye by Ivana Sajko

I read this book about a man on a train to Berlin while I was on a flight to Barcelona. I thought this slim novel would be the perfect travel book; I was wrong. Don’t read this in an enclosed space. Sajko’s prose leaves you no room to breathe. Each long, winding sentence yanks you through the memories of a man whose life is constrained by a succession of world crises. I’ve never felt so useless in the face of history. I can’t recommend this book enough.

  • Evander Reyes, Communications Director

The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout

If you know me, you know I love everything Elizabeth Strout writes. Her latest novel, out in May, is a beautiful and haunting exploration of the way secrets can fester, and when they emerge, upend everything. I was immediately hooked by the authority of the voice on the page, and the beauty of the sentences. I love this novel with all my heart!

  • Denne Michele Norris, Executive Director and Publisher

The post 15 Books We Read and Loved This Summer appeared first on Electric Literature.

title: Sophie, Meg Mason'ın Standing There (Orada Durmak) incelemesi – gerçek hayattaki yazarların küçük rolleriyle edebi bir saplantı hikayesi
desc: A heartbroken woman becomes fixated on a famous writer in this witty, touching follow-up to Sorrow and BlissThe protagonist of Meg Mason’s new book, the follow-up to the 2020 tragicomedy Sorrow and Bl...
content:
A heartbroken woman becomes fixated on a famous writer in this witty, touching follow-up to Sorrow and Bliss

The protagonist of Meg Mason’s new book, the follow-up to the 2020 tragicomedy Sorrow and Bliss, is an invisible woman. She might well be standing there but you won’t notice her. She’s a techie at literary festivals – the person who shuffles up to a famous writer a few minutes before their event and apologetically slides a microphone cable down their shirt while they’re making small talk with the chair or accepting a bottle of room-temperature mineral water from an anxious publicist.

No man is a hero to his valet, and no writer is a hero to the technical staff lurking in the wings of a venue. Mason’s opening pages present a teasing but not quite libellous series of cameos from real writers: George Saunders deciding at an inconsiderately late stage to insist on swapping his headset for a lapel mic; Ann Patchett being frosty with a fan; Mick Herron accidentally stepping on someone’s foot and not apologising.

title: Tarihsel Kurgunuzla Çıkmanın Sekiz Basit Kuralı
desc:
This first appeared in Lit Hub’s Craft of Writing newsletter—sign up here.
Consider these opening lines. Their source is far from obscure, so there’s a good chance you’ll recognize them right away. Ta...
content:
This first appeared in Lit Hub’s Craft of Writing newsletter—sign up here.

Consider these opening lines. Their source is far from obscure, so there’s a good chance you’ll recognize them right away. Take a moment over them anyway:

“So now get up.”

Felled, dazed, silent, he has fallen; knocked full length on the cobbles of the yard. His head turns sideways; his eyes are turned towards the gate, as if someone might arrive to help him out.

One blow, properly placed, could kill him now.

The excerpt is taken, of course, from the first page of Wolf Hall, for which Hilary Mantel won the Booker Prize in 2009. Not exactly a deep cut as historical fiction goes, but for my purposes a near-ideal example.

Of what? Well, in the rules I’m about to set out, I warn of the ways in which we can get historical fiction wrong. And Wolf Hall—from its opening lines to its final page—is as complete a demonstration of technical excellence as we could wish for. We’ll discuss some examples in just a moment, but first a bit of procedural housekeeping.

You will object, I’m sure, that literary craft is infinitely nuanced and that rules like the ones below are reductive and arbitrary. Plus, you might argue, they get broken all the time, and by unassailable giants of the genre.

The thing about literary giants, though, is that they tend to know what they’re doing. When they break a rule, they generally understand it thoroughly and weigh their decision carefully. When you break one you’re just doing it wrong. Good? Good.

Yes, Susanna Clarke did it, but (a) she did a lot more besides, and (b) you are not Susanna Clarke.

Also, one last thing: In case anyone missed my tiresome play on words, the “dating” in the title refers to the various techniques you can use to situate your novel in time and place. You may be familiar with some or all of these, but you should still pay attention. Most require a light touch and a clear notion of the desired effect. Some, though, should be approached like they just oozed from a meteorite in a puddle of hissing slime.

Okay, team, let’s have fun out there!

Rule No. 1: Go Easy on the Period Diction
Language is what books are made of, and all prose and dialogue must be outfitted in some sort of style. If your setting comes stocked with pungently recognizable idiom—with prithees and sires and by-your-leaves—there’s a temptation to help yourself in great armfuls.

But look again at the Mantel excerpt. Her chosen milieu is Tudor England, and she has a scholar’s intimacy with the flavors of Early Modern English then in use. But a modern novel crusted stiff with pre-Shakespearean locutions would no longer be a modern novel; it would be a wearying parlor trick.

Mantel cleaves instead to a felicitous simplicity, to constructions that achieve consonance with the period but stop short of mimicry. She begins as she means to go on. The boy on the ground is Thomas Cromwell, who will one day be Lord Privy Seal and the unsparing architect of the English Reformation. His public utterances will brim with courtly niceties, and with legal and ecclesiastical arcana. Mantel will show us just enough of all that when the time comes.

For now he is just a boy, cowering before his brutish father. His world was not wide before, and now it has shrunk to a few miserable particulars: a blunt taunt, a cobbled yard, a beating. Now as then, the words for such things are simple.

Rule No. 2: Spell Like a Normal Person
Say you’ve pitched up in England at some point from the early Georgian era onwards, or in America a little later on. You’ll have made the exciting discovery that your primary sources include actual novels.

Let’s imagine, too, that in a spirit of dauntless thoroughness you’ve sought out the unmodernized editions of Defoe or Fielding or whoever. It’s a worthy philological undertaking, if nothing else. Our modern conventions of orthography, typography and speech-marking took a long time to solidify, and it’s instructive to see that process unfold.

It’s not without its perils, though, particularly when you reach the relatively familiar climes of the nineteenth century. Here you’ll feel mostly at home, and when your eye is caught by such archaisms as Jane Austen’s spellings you might find yourself wondering what harm it could do. You certainly wouldn’t be the first.

But listen, this is not the way. You are not going to fast-track your way to authentic Regency by putting “chuse” for “choose.” Yes, Susanna Clarke did it, but (a) she did a lot more besides, and (b) you are not Susanna Clarke.

Rule No. 3: Don’t Use Your Research to Accessorize
You’re writing a historical novel, which means you’ve been putting in some serious hours at the library. (You have, haven’t you? Because this is in no way optional.)

And having done all that research, you might form the view that none of it should be wasted. Like, that one detail about the turning radius of Shillibeer’s Omnibus—that has to go somewhere, surely? The answer, alas, is usually no.

You should read widely about your period and deeply about those particulars that naturally arise in your story. Most of that reading, though, should be kept off the page or confined to the gentlest cross-hatching. That way, the reader will attend gladly to the details you do alight on, having come to trust that they matter.

Treat the rest of your shiny trinkets like in that mirror-twirl trick when you’re getting ready to go out. If it catches your eye immediately, take it off.

Rule No. 4: The Past Is Another Country, but Your Characters Live There
Choosing a point of view is a consequential decision for any novelist, but in historical fiction the stakes are heightened. Omniscient narrators are a thing, to be sure, and they were much more of a thing in centuries past, along with chatty and freely moralizing perorations to the Gentle Reader. However, managing such conspicuous anachronisms requires consummate skill (see Eleanor Catton’s The Luminaries for how it’s done), so don’t say you weren’t warned.

I most cases, though, you’ll be using either the first person or the near-default close third. This means that in any given scene, you’ll be relating the proceedings from the perspective of a specific individual shaped by highly particular circumstances. That individual should want, care about and notice a closely circumscribed subset of things.

Her own clothing? Maybe, if some occasion requires it and she has the means and leisure to change it. The streetscape, the shopfronts, the hansom cabs, the coal smoke, the gaslights, the stink? Unless she’s new here, then not without some particular reason. Just like you, she’s probably preoccupied with something (so tell us that instead), and just like you, most of what she sees every day is all but invisible. Choose carefully.

Rule No. 5: Stop Worldbuilding Like It’s Westeros, Dammit
All this pontificating might give you the wrong impression, so I should make it clear that I, too, am a trash human with terrible habits. Exhibit A: Your boy watches way too many video essays on YouTube. These are all far too long, and too many are about fantasy fiction and its weird fixation on the Everlasting Medieval.

I bring this up because I’ve developed a pet theory, which is that the quasi-historicism of fantasy fiction has opened a portal to a parallel genre, infecting historical fiction with Certain Tendencies. Among these are the egregious outbursts of exposition that are tolerated in the cause of “worldbuilding,” as if having an official term somehow makes it okay.

There’s no excuse for wheeling in some talkative NPC just to explain why the townsfolk are acting skittish. As with most technical problems, find a solution that’s natural and unobtrusive.

This carry-on usually occurs under flimsy pretexts. “We had all heard the tales,” someone will begin, and the tales that follow will bespeak an oral tradition of near-miraculous efficiency. We will learn of the ills wrought by this or that king; such-and-such a usurper; one bunch or another of interlopers, of idolaters, of haughty conquerors, of benighted rabble. The glories of some former age may be lamented, and our sympathies directed to parties judged righteous or wronged.

Decades, even centuries, may be encompassed by these marvelously comprehensive surveys. Some readers may even welcome them, on the grounds that there’s just so much to cover and it’s, like, hella convenient. That’s no excuse. This isn’t Elden Ring, and there isn’t supposed to be a hotkey for lore. Reveal your world as someone experiences it, or don’t reveal it at all.

Rule No. 6: Stop Set-Dressing Like It’s Downton Abbey
Again, I don’t issue this edict from some kind of high horse. I still know every single number in that one musical episode of Buffy, so it’s not like I don’t love me some high-fructose TV. I’m not coming for anyone’s comfort reads either. There’s a place in this world for book covers with someone’s lush decolletage and a font from a wedding menu.

Given that you’re six points deep into this particular list, however, I’m going to assume that Bridgerton is not the vibe you’re going for. And at the grownup table, sad to say, you don’t get to blow the budget on wardrobe and production design then call it good.

No one’s saying your text has to be barren of ornament. There can be sumptuous frocks and silk wall hangings, but the gaze that gets drawn to them should not be your own. Because again, who is doing the seeing here?

Is it someone awed and out of their element? Someone briskly assessing workmanship or disparaging a social inferior? Someone taking brusque possession while sneering at all this decadence?

Moments like these may occur, but they must arise in the natural course of your story. Otherwise, make do like the rest of us and save your fire takes on eveningwear for posting about the Met Gala.

Rule No. 7: Your Characters Aren’t Tour Guides
Worldbuilding aside, you should be wary of any explanations that arrive at oddly convenient moments. There is the common practice, for instance, whereby some minor character is briefly seconded to a protagonist’s service, only to be dispensed with again once the required payload of information has been delivered.

These are perfunctory roles by definition, so lackeys of one kind or another are often favored. Innkeepers may be pressed into service, or drivers, porters, errand boys or grooms. Discontented domestics are perennial favorites too, as are enterprising sex workers. Anyone will do, really, as long as they stay long enough to say something useful, but not so long that they become a nuisance.

And look, I get it: exposition is hard and perfect verisimilitude is neither possible nor desirable; we all make our small accommodations. There’s no excuse, though, for wheeling in some talkative NPC just to explain why the townsfolk are acting skittish. As with most technical problems, find a solution that’s natural and unobtrusive. That’s pretty much your whole job.

Rule No. 8: Historical Fiction Is Still Contemporary Fiction
I’ve saved this rule for last because it’s the one nearest my heart. If I have indulged myself elsewhere in this list, veering now and then towards puckishness or provocation, in this I am entirely sincere.

As historical novelists, like writers of any kind, we should be faithful to our subject and to our reader. Yet subject and setting are not the same, only closely entwined. We do justice if we can to the substrates of our chosen worlds, but we make no claims to true scholarship. We are inventors of moments, of days, of lives, and truthful only after our own fashion.

We are attentive visitors to the past, yes, and we tread its ground carefully, but we are not museum-keepers or archaeologists. We do not unearth cities but remake them; do not raise the dead but summon in their place the newly living.

In doing so, we never conjure the same spectre twice, and it is no fault that we catch our own voices in theirs; that they wear our many skins and tremble with our many kinds of love. We honor their imagined worlds, but we make them for the one we live in.

_______________________________________________________


The Naming of the Birds by Paraic O’Donnell is available via Tin House.

desc:
Claire Stapleton’s Don’t Be Evil, Kimon de Greef’s The Ego Trip, and Dave Ziren’s The People’s Historian all feature among the best reviewed nonfiction titles of the month.
Brought to you by Book Mark...
content:
Claire Stapleton’s Don’t Be Evil, Kimon de Greef’s The Ego Trip, and Dave Ziren’s The People’s Historian all feature among the best reviewed nonfiction titles of the month.

Brought to you by Book Marks, Lit Hub’s home for book reviews.

*

1. Don’t Be Evil: Bad Bosses, Fake Promises, and My Escape from Big Tech by Claire Stapleton
(William Morrow and Company)

4 Rave • 1 Positive • 1 Mixed

“A blunt account of one woman’s transformation from eager-to-please corporate striver to clear-eyed activist. It well earns its place alongside other recent accounts of the misdeeds of Big Tech like Sarah Wynn-Williams’ Careless People and Anna Wiener’s Uncanny Valley … Books like Stapleton’s will at least arm people determined to reform them with information they’ll need to make that effort.”

–Harvey Freedenberg (BookPage)

2. The Ego Trip: Psychedelic Toads, a Trail of Deaths, and the Guru Who Peddled Transcendence by Kimon de Greef
(Doubleday)

4 Rave • 1 Positive

“A marvelous trip, exploring centuries of the Seris’ tribulations, the growth of commercial toad milking in a region dominated by narco gangsters, quarrels among rival gurus and competition between the sons of an English countess and a German baroness to develop 5-MeO-DMT into a pharmaceutical.”

–Annie Bartlett (BookPage)

3. The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State by Jill Lepore
(Liveright)

3 Rave • 2 Positive • 1 Mixed

“Staggering, sobering, yet essential reading for all who want to understand the arc of this increasingly digital, online, corporate, and out-of-control world.”

–Carol Haggas (Booklist)

4. Days of Miracle and Wonder: Paul Simon and the Trials and Triumphs of Graceland by Ahley Kahn
(Atria)

4 Rave • 1 Mixed

“What a welcome surprise … Has only made me appreciate the album’s intricacies and paradoxes all the more … Kahn lets his historical actors speak for themselves as often as possible, collecting a remarkably wide array of voices for so short a book.”

–Mark Braude (The New York Times Book Review)

5. The People’s Historian: The Outsized Life of Howard Zinn by Dave Zirin
(Dutton)

2 Rave • 3 Positive • 2 Mixed

“Rousing … It’s a wonderful portrait of a historian who reshaped America’s understanding of its potential for change.”

–Publishers Weekly
